text: A model nobody can understand or reproduce is a liability. Six months from now, a colleague, or you, will ask: what data was this trained on, how good is it, and what should I not use it for? Documentation answers those questions before anyone asks.

A modeling project needs four small documents. A README that says how to run it. A model card that says what the model is, what data it used, its numbers and its limits. A decisions log of dated choices and why you made them. And a requirements file with exact library versions.

Here is the top of a real model card template. It states the purpose, and just as important, a non purpose: not for pricing or credit decisions. Then the data section, including a data fingerprint: a short hash that shows whether two people have the same data.

Notice the curly braces. They are placeholders that code fills in. You collect the facts in a dictionary: row count, seed, test AUC, library versions. Then template dot format fills the card, so the numbers can never drift from the model.

The rendered card for our illustrative churn model reports a test AUC of point eight zero two, recall of point four four seven, and a churn rate of sixty-four percent in the riskiest twenty percent. It also reports AUC by contract type.

The decisions log entry is short. Date, context, the decision, why, and when to revisit. Here we chose logistic regression over a random forest because its cross validated AUC was higher, point eight zero six versus point seven eight two, and it is easier to explain.

Then the reproducibility checklist. Set random state everywhere. Freeze versions with pip freeze. Save the fitted pipeline with joblib, and record the scikit-learn version. Finally, write limitations that are specific and checkable, not vague. Honest limits make reviewers trust the rest.
